claim: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancers (mCRPCs) are treated with therapies that antagonize the androgen receptor (AR).
source: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancers (mCRPCs) are treated with therapies that antagonize the androgen receptor (AR).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about mCRPC treatment.

claim: Nearly all patients develop resistance to AR-targeted therapies (ARTs).
source: Nearly all patients develop resistance to AR-targeted therapies (ARTs).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about treatment resistance in mCRPC.

claim: CREB5 was identified as an upregulated target gene in human mCRPC that promoted resistance to all clinically approved ART.
source: Our previous work identified CREB5 as an upregulated target gene in human mCRPC that promoted resistance to all clinically approved ART.
evidence: This claim references previous work by the authors (Hwang et al., 2019).

claim: Cells overexpressing CREB5 demonstrate extensive reprogramming of nuclear protein–protein interactions in response to the ART agent enzalutamide.
source: Integrating ChIP-seq and rapid immunoprecipitation and mass spectroscopy of endogenous proteins, we report that cells overexpressing CREB5 demonstrate extensive reprogramming of nuclear protein–protein interactions in response to the ART agent enzalutamide.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RIME experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CREB5 physically interacts with AR, the pioneering factor FOXA1, and other known co-factors of AR and FOXA1 at transcription regulatory elements recently found to be active in mCRPC patients.
source: Specifically, CREB5 physically interacts with AR, the pioneering actor FOXA1, and other known co-factors of AR and FOXA1 at transcription regulatory elements recently found to be active in mCRPC patients.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RIME experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GRHL2 and HOXB13 are CREB5/FOXA1 co-interacting nuclear factors that have critical functions for AR transcription.
source: We identified a subset of CREB5/FOXA1 co-interacting nuclear factors that have critical functions for AR transcription (GRHL2, HOXB13)
evidence: This is supported by RIME data and functional validation experiments in the manuscript.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC are CREB5/FOXA1 co-interacting nuclear factors that regulated cell viability and ART resistance.
source: We identified a subset of CREB5/FOXA1 co-interacting nuclear factors that have critical functions for AR transcription (GRHL2, HOXB13) while others (TBX3, NFIC) regulated cell viability and ART resistance
evidence: This is supported by RIME data and functional validation experiments in the manuscript.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC were amplified or overexpressed in mCRPC.
source: We identified a subset of CREB5/FOXA1 co-interacting nuclear factors that have critical functions for AR transcription (GRHL2, HOXB13) while others (TBX3, NFIC) regulated cell viability and ART resistance and were amplified or overexpressed in mCRPC.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic and expression data from mCRPC patient samples.

claim: CREB5 was associated with Wnt signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transitions.
source: Upon examining the nuclear protein interactions and the impact of CREB5 expression on the mCRPC patient transcriptome, we found that CREB5 was associated with Wnt signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transitions
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis of RIME data and gene expression correlation analysis in mCRPC samples.

claim: Wnt signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transitions are implicated in CREB5/FOXA1-mediated ART resistance.
source: Upon examining the nuclear protein interactions and the impact of CREB5 expression on the mCRPC patient transcriptome, we found that CREB5 was associated with Wnt signaling and epithelial to mesenchymal transitions, implicating these pathways in CREB5/FOXA1-mediated ART resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the association of CREB5 with these pathways and its role in ART resistance.

claim: The androgen receptor (AR) plays a fundamental role in the development and function of the prostate.
source: The androgen receptor (AR) plays a fundamental role in the development and function of the prostate.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AR function.

claim: AR transcriptional activity is required for the initiation and progression of prostate cancer and remains critical in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC).
source: AR transcriptional activity is required for the initiation and progression of prostate cancer and remains critical in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) (Abida et al., 2019; Armenia et al., 2018; Grasso et al., 2012; He et al., 2021; Robinson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The standard of care for patients with mCRPC is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and AR-targeted therapies (ARTs).
source: The standard of care for patients with mCRPC is androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and AR-targeted therapies (ARTs).
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about mCRPC treatment.

claim: ADT and ART initially induce responses and lengthen the survival of mCRPC patients.
source: While ADT and ART initially induce responses and lengthen the survival of mCRPC patients, intrinsic or acquired resistance continues to be a substantial clinical obstacle.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about treatment response in mCRPC.

claim: Intrinsic or acquired resistance to ADT and ART continues to be a substantial clinical obstacle.
source: While ADT and ART initially induce responses and lengthen the survival of mCRPC patients, intrinsic or acquired resistance continues to be a substantial clinical obstacle.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about treatment resistance in mCRPC.

claim: A subset of resistant mCRPC harbor AR genomic alterations through mutations, copy number gain, enhancer amplification, as well as increased resistant transcript variants (ARV7).
source: Recent studies of mCRPC patients resistant to second-generation ART and ADT have identified that a subset of the resistant mCRPC harbor AR genomic alterations through mutations, copy number gain, enhancer amplification, as well as increased resistant transcript variants (ARV7) (Bubley and Balk, 2017; Henzler et al., 2016; Takeda et al., 2018; Viswanathan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Resistance to ART also occurs through mechanisms including upregulation of cell cycle genes.
source: Other clinical and functional studies together demonstrate that resistance also occurs through mechanisms, including upregulation of cell cycle genes (Comstock et al., 2013; Han et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Resistance to ART also occurs through upregulation of the proto-oncogene MYC.
source: Other clinical and functional studies together demonstrate that resistance also occurs through mechanisms, including upregulation of cell cycle genes (Comstock et al., 2013; Han et al., 2017) and/or the proto-oncogene MYC (Abida et al., 2019; Armenia et al., 2018; Bernard et al., 2003; Grasso et al., 2012; Robinson et al., 2015; Sharma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Selective activation of pathways such as epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGFβ and Wnt has been recently identified from profiling mCRPC patients that became resistant to second-generation ART or ADT.
source: In addition, selective activation of pathways such as epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), TGFβ and Wnt has been recently identified from profiling mCRPC patient become resistant to second-generation ART or ADT (Alumkal et al., 2020; He et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: AR activity in prostate tissue is regulated by AR co-factors such as HOXB13 and FOXA1 at AR binding sites (ARBs).
source: AR activity in prostate tissue is regulated by AR co-factors such as HOXB13 and FOXA1 at AR binding sites (ARBs) (Pomerantz et al., 2015; Pomerantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 is a co-factor with both pioneering and transcription functions.
source: ChIP-seq experiments have demonstrated that FOXA1, a co-factor with both pioneering and transcription functions, binds to distinct sites and has different protein interactions that is dependent on the disease stage and pathological phenotype (Baca et al., 2021; Pomerantz et al., 2015; Pomerantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 binds to distinct sites and has different protein interactions that is dependent on the disease stage and pathological phenotype.
source: ChIP-seq experiments have demonstrated that FOXA1, a co-factor with both pioneering and transcription functions, binds to distinct sites and has different protein interactions that is dependent on the disease stage and pathological phenotype (Baca et al., 2021; Pomerantz et al., 2015; Pomerantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Genomic alterations of FOXA1 promote ART resistance.
source: Recent studies indicate that genomic alterations of FOXA1 promote ART resistance (Adams et al., 2019; Baca et al., 2021; Parolia et al., 2019; Shah and Brown, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 function remains functionally relevant even as mCRPC differentiate into aggressive variants that no longer require AR signaling, such as neuroendocrine prostate cancer.
source: We have shown that FOXA1 function remains functionally relevant even as mCRPC differentiate into aggressive variants that no longer require AR signaling, such as neuroendocrine prostate cancer (Baca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study by the authors.

claim: The transcriptional factor cAMP-responsive element binding protein 5 (CREB5) promoted resistance to FDA-approved ART, enzalutamide, darolutamide and apalutamide.
source: We have previously demonstrated that the transcriptional factor cAMP-responsive element binding protein 5 (CREB5) promoted resistance to FDA-approved ART, enzalutamide, darolutamide and apalutamide (Hwang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study by the authors.

claim: CREB5 has been associated with progression of ovarian, colorectal, and breast cancers.
source: CREB5 has also been associated with progression of cancers, including ovarian, colorectal, and breast (Bhardwaj et al., 2017; He et al., 2017; Molnár et al., 2018; Qi and Ding, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: The molecular mechanisms by which CREB5 promotes resistance in mCRPC or general tumorigenesis remains unclear.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms by which CREB5 promotes resistance in mCRPC or general tumorigenesis remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Overexpression of CREB5 reduced viability (Z = –1.3) in standard cultures.
source: Upon re-examining the data, we found that unlike in ADT/ART, overexpression of CREB5 reduced viability (Z = –1.3) in standard cultures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data from a genome-scale screen shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CREB5 overexpression exhibited robust differential Z-scores when comparing the treated arm (Z = +14.5) to the control arm (Z = –1.3).
source: The Z-scores, which represent relative proliferation effects compared to all 17,255 ORFs, exhibited robust differentials when comparing the treated arm in comparison to the control arm (Z = +14.5 and –1.3).
evidence: This is supported by data from a genome-scale screen.

claim: CDK4 or CDK6 promoted cell fitness regardless of treatment conditions.
source: This observation contrasted to other genes that mediate resistance to ART, such as CDK4 or CDK6, which promoted cell fitness regardless of treatment conditions.
evidence: This is supported by data from a genome-scale screen.

claim: CREB5 had the greatest differential viability effect after low androgen and enzalutamide treatment among ORFs.
source: Among ORFs, CREB5 had the greatest differential viability effect after low androgen and enzalutamide treatment (Supplementary file 1, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data from a genome-scale screen.

claim: CREB5 binding sites segregated into lost (n = 5392), retained (n = 12,432), or gained (n = 12,144) categories in the enzalutamide condition compared to the pretreatment condition.
source: CREB5 overexpression induced a robust differential phenotype (Figure 1B), in which lost (n = 5392), retained (n = 12,432), or gained (n = 12,144) CREB5 binding sites were tallied in the enzalutamide condition compared to the pretreatment condition.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The elements in which CREB5 retained or gained sites were statistically significantly enriched of other nuclear proteins including AR, FOXA1, and HOXB13.
source: We observed that the elements in which CREB5 retained or gained sites were statistically significantly enriched of other nuclear proteins in which ChIP-seq had been performed in prostate cancer cell lines. This included binding elements (AR, FOXA1, HOXB13) that we previously demonstrated through ChIP-seq experiments (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by GIGGLE analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Retained or gained sequences nominated well-studied regulators or co-factors of AR such as GRHL2, EP300, and SMARCA4.
source: In addition, we also identify that retained or gained sequences nominated well-studied regulators or co-factors of AR such as GRHL2 (Paltoglou et al., 2017), EP300 (Yu et al., 2020), and SMARCA4 (Launonen et al., 2021; Marshall et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by GIGGLE analysis and cited studies.

claim: Genetic ablation of AR or FOXA1 reduced viability of CREB5-overexpressing cells.
source: In confirmation of previous findings, the genetic ablation of AR or FOXA1 reduced viability of CREB5-overexpressing cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Hwang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a cited study.

claim: CREB5-bound unique peptides segregated into lost (n = 77), retained (n = 222), and gained groups (n = 207) when comparing control to enzalutamide-treated conditions.
source: When we compared the analyzed RIME binding profiles of the control to the enzalutamide-treated conditions, analogous to the ChIP-seq experiments, we found the CREB5-bound unique peptides also segregated into lost (n = 77), retained (n = 222), and gained groups (n = 207) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both GIGGLE and RIME approaches nominated known AR interactions including EP300, FOXA1, and GRHL2.
source: From this, we found both approaches nominated known AR interactions (EP300, FOXA1, and GRHL2).
evidence: This is supported by GIGGLE and RIME data.

claim: CREB5 binding dynamically responds to ART treatment.
source: Overall, these parallel approaches demonstrate that CREB5 binding dynamically responds to ART treatment.
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq and RIME data showing changes in CREB5 binding and interactions upon enzalutamide treatment.

claim: The retained or gained RIME interactions indicate CREB5 may interact with distinct sets of co-factors, some of which are AR associated, to promote ART resistance.
source: Moreover, the retained or gained RIME interactions indicate CREB5 may interact with distinct sets of co-factors, some of which are AR associated, to promote ART resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on RIME data showing retained and gained interactions.

claim: Overexpressing CREB3 conferred significantly weaker resistance to enzalutamide compared to CREB5.
source: In prior work in LNCaP cells, we found that overexpressing CREB3, a related CREB family member, conferred significantly weaker resistance to enzalutamide, and therefore serves as a useful control to understand CREB5 functions in resistance (Hwang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study by the authors.

claim: The overall RIME profiles of CREB5 and FOXA1 exhibited a positive correlation (R = 0.394).
source: The overall RIME profiles of CREB5 and FOXA1 were compared and exhibited a positive correlation (R = 0.394), while those of CREB3 with either CREB5 or FOXA1 lacked correlation (R = 0.0332, –0.0498) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The RIME profiles of CREB3 with either CREB5 or FOXA1 lacked correlation (R = 0.0332, –0.0498).
source: The overall RIME profiles of CREB5 and FOXA1 were compared and exhibited a positive correlation (R = 0.394), while those of CREB3 with either CREB5 or FOXA1 lacked correlation (R = 0.0332, –0.0498) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CREB5 and FOXA1 shared a total of 504 protein interactions at chromatin.
source: At the peptide level, we found that CREB5 and FOXA1 shared a total of 504 protein interactions at chromatin, and of these 504, 335 did not interact with CREB3.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data.

claim: Of the 504 shared CREB5 and FOXA1 protein interactions, 335 did not interact with CREB3.
source: At the peptide level, we found that CREB5 and FOXA1 shared a total of 504 protein interactions at chromatin, and of these 504, 335 did not interact with CREB3.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data.

claim: CREB3 and FOXA1 shared only 83 unique interactions.
source: While almost three times the number of CREB3 peptides were detected relative to CREB5, CREB3 and FOXA1 shared only 83 unique interactions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Regardless of ART, more than 90% of CREB5-bound sites were FOXA1 bound.
source: By analyzing ChIP-seq experiments that targeted either CREB5 or FOXA1, we found that regardless of ART, CREB5 and FOXA1 shared a strong degree of interactions as more than 90% of CREB5-bound sites were FOXA1 bound (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AR binding sites are reprogrammed during tumorigenesis and progression.
source: Pomerantz et al. have recently demonstrated that AR binding sites are reprogrammed during tumorigenesis and progression (Pomerantz et al., 2015; Pomerantz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: CREB5 bound ARBs in prostate cancer (12.7%) or mCRPC (8.6%) tissue at higher rates as compared to normal prostate ARBs (0.2%).
source: When considering the subset of ARBs specific to progression, CREB5 indeed bound ARBs in prostate cancer (12.7%) or mCRPC (8.6%) tissue at higher rates as compared to normal prostate ARBs (0.2%) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Almost all CREB5-bound sites were also observed in mCRPCs and were FOXA1 bound.
source: Almost all CREB5-bound sites were also observed in mCRPCs and were FOXA1 bound (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CREB5 and FOXA1 engage a similar subset of proteins in cells with ART resistance.
source: Taken together these observations demonstrate that CREB5 and FOXA1 engage a similar subset of proteins in cells with ART resistance and these interactions are enriched at ARBs or FOXA1 binding sites in mCRPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on RIME and ChIP-seq data.

claim: CREB5 and FOXA1 interactions are enriched at ARBs or FOXA1 binding sites in mCRPC.
source: Taken together these observations demonstrate that CREB5 and FOXA1 engage a similar subset of proteins in cells with ART resistance and these interactions are enriched at ARBs or FOXA1 binding sites in mCRPC.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis.

claim: The B-Zip and L-Zip domains are highly homologous in CREB and ATF family members.
source: Based on sequence alignment, the B-Zip and L-Zip domains are highly homologous in CREB and ATF family members (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The B-Zip and L-Zip domains regulate binding to DNA- and CREB co-factors.
source: Based on sequence alignment, the B-Zip and L-Zip domains are highly homologous in CREB and ATF family members (Figure 3A) and regulate binding to DNA- and CREB co-factors (Dwarki et al., 1990; Luo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Several leucine residues within the B-Zip and L-Zip domains regulate transcriptional activity and heterodimerization with the transcription factors JUN and FOS in vitro.
source: Within the B-Zip and L-Zip domains, several leucine residues regulate transcriptional activity and heterodimerization with the transcription factors JUN and FOS in vitro (Fuchs and Ronai, 1999; Nomura et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Cells expressing L431P and L434P CREB5 mutants proliferated similarly to cells expressing luciferase controls in cell doubling assays performed in low androgen media containing enzalutamide.
source: We expressed these CREB5 variants in LNCaP cells (Figure 3B) and found that despite robust expression of L431P and L434P CREB5, cells expressing these mutants proliferated similarly to cells expressing luciferase controls in cell doubling assays performed in low androgen media containing enzalutamide (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: L431P and L434P CREB5 mutants lacked interactions critical for ART resistance.
source: We expressed these CREB5 variants in LNCaP cells (Figure 3B) and found that despite robust expression of L431P and L434P CREB5, cells expressing these mutants proliferated similarly to cells expressing luciferase controls in cell doubling assays performed in low androgen media containing enzalutamide (Figure 3B), indicating L431P and L434P CREB5 lacked interactions critical for ART resistance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of proliferation advantage in cells expressing these mutants.

claim: There was a striking correlation between the interaction profiles of CREB5 and CREB5 L434P (R = 0.834).
source: At approximately the same average peptide counts of CREB5 (8) and L434 CREB5 (7.5), we found a striking correlation between the interaction profiles of CREB5 and CREB5 L434P (R = 0.834).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data.

claim: The L434P mutant binds the same proteins as wild-type CREB5.
source: At approximately the same average peptide counts of CREB5 (8) and L434 CREB5 (7.5), we found a striking correlation between the interaction profiles of CREB5 and CREB5 L434P (R = 0.834). This observation indicated that this CREB5 mutant binds the same proteins as the L434P mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high correlation between CREB5 and L434P RIME profiles.

claim: There was no correlation between CREB3 and wild-type CREB5 (R = −0.0581).
source: In parallel, we failed to find a correlation between CREB3 and wild-type CREB5 (R = −0.0581) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Smaller differences were found between wild-type and L434P CREB5 for AR, FOXA1, and HOXB13 interactions.
source: When examining the interactions of wild-type and L434P CREB5, we found smaller differences between AR, FOXA1, and HOXB13 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NFIC and TBX3 peptides were detected preferentially in cells expressing wild-type CREB5 as compared to L434P or CREB3.
source: Outside of AR co-factors, we detected unique peptide signals at comparable levels with AR, FOXA1, and HOXB13, including NFIC, TBX3 (Figure 3D). We detected peptides from these proteins preferentially in cells expressing wild-type CREB5 as compared to L434P or CREB3.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In AR-positive cell lines, TBX3 and NFIC exhibited a pattern of cell line dependencies as observed for FOXA1.
source: We found that in AR-positive cell lines (Figure 4A, left) TBX3 and NFIC exhibited a pattern of cell line dependencies as observed for FOXA1.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genome-scale RNAi screens shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In AR-negative cell lines, TBX3 exhibited no clear dependency, while NFIC exhibited modest dependency as compared to FOXA1.
source: When examining AR-negative cell lines (Figure 4A, right), we found that TBX3 exhibited no clear dependency, while NFIC exhibited modest dependency as compared to FOXA1.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genome-scale RNAi screens shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC regulate prostate cancer cell viability in the AR setting.
source: This close correlation of TBX3 and NFIC dependency with that observed for FOXA1 supports the conclusion that TBX3 and NFIC regulate prostate cancer cell viability in the AR setting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation of TBX3 and NFIC dependency with FOXA1 in AR-positive cell lines.

claim: NFIC and TBX3 ranked among the strongest dependencies in prostate cancer cell lines while exhibiting limited overall dependency in other 495 cell lines.
source: Furthermore, upon computing the average dependency scores in DEMETER, we found that NFIC and TBX3 ranked among the strongest dependencies in these prostate cancer cell lines while exhibiting limited overall dependency in the other 495 cell lines (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DEMETER dependency scores shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The relative dependencies of NFIC and TBX3 were comparable to the strongest gene dependencies, such as FOXA1 and HOXB13.
source: The relative dependencies of NFIC and TBX3 were comparable to the strongest gene dependencies, such as FOXA1 and HOXB13, found in previous studies (Pomerantz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DEMETER dependency scores and a cited study.

claim: Suppression of TBX3 or NFIC using two shRNAs reduced the viability of CREB5-overexpressing LNCaP cells to the same extent as two positive control shRNAs that targeted FOXA1.
source: We found that suppression of TBX3 or NFIC using two shRNAs, as compared to a negative control (GFP), reduced the viability of CREB5-overexpressing LNCaP cells to the same extent as two positive control shRNAs that targeted FOXA1.
evidence: This is supported by RNAi-mediated gene depletion experiments.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC are required for optimal viability of CREB5 cells in the presence of enzalutamide.
source: This observation indicates that TBX3 and NFIC, like FOXA1, are required for optimal viability of CREB5 cells in the presence of enzalutamide.
evidence: This is an inference based on RNAi-mediated gene depletion experiments.

claim: sgRNAs against FOXA1, TBX3, or NFIC all reduced protein levels and decreased viability in a cell line model that spontaneously acquired enzalutamide resistance.
source: In this cell line, we expressed three distinct sgRNAs that depleted FOXA1 or two sgRNAs that ablated TBX3 or NFIC, and we found that the sgRNAs against FOXA1, TBX3, or NFIC all reduced protein levels and decreased viability (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene depletion experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There was statistically significant enrichment of FOXA1 binding motifs in TBX3 or NFIC binding sites identified in experiments on breast or prostate cancer cell lines.
source: Based on motif enrichment analyses of the TBX3 or NFIC binding sites, we observed statistically significant enrichment of FOXA1 binding motifs identified in experiments on breast or prostate cancer cell lines (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NFIC also bound B-Zip motifs.
source: Like CREB5, NFIC also bound B-Zip motifs.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC genomic amplifications together represented up to 13.3% of prostate cancers.
source: We found that TBX3 and NFIC genomic amplifications together represented up to 13.3% of prostate cancers, in which notably higher amplification rates were observed in mCRPC studies as opposed to those sampling primary prostate cancer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic data from cBioPortal shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Higher amplification rates of TBX3 and NFIC were observed in mCRPC studies as opposed to those sampling primary prostate cancer.
source: We found that TBX3 and NFIC genomic amplifications together represented up to 13.3% of prostate cancers, in which notably higher amplification rates were observed in mCRPC studies as opposed to those sampling primary prostate cancer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic data from cBioPortal shown in Figure 5A.

claim: TBX3, NFIC, and FOXA1 were amplified or overexpressed in 7, 3, and 7% of mCRPC samples, respectively.
source: Upon examining expression and amplification data mCRPC samples (Abida et al., 2019), we found that TBX3, NFIC, and FOXA1 were amplified or overexpressed in 7, 3, and 7% of mCRPC samples, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic and expression data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a robust positive correlation between FOXA1 with TBX3 (Spearman's correlation: 0.416; q-value: 1.48e-7).
source: Of the 209 samples with expression data, we found a robust positive correlation between FOXA1 with TBX3 (Spearman's correlation: 0.416; q-value: 1.48e-7) or NFIC (Spearman's correlation: 0.536; q-value: 4.34e-15) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of expression data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was a robust positive correlation between FOXA1 with NFIC (Spearman's correlation: 0.536; q-value: 4.34e-15).
source: Of the 209 samples with expression data, we found a robust positive correlation between FOXA1 with TBX3 (Spearman's correlation: 0.416; q-value: 1.48e-7) or NFIC (Spearman's correlation: 0.536; q-value: 4.34e-15) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of expression data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC were nuclear proteins associated with CREB5, FOXA1, and functionally impacted prostate cancer cell viability and ART resistance even absent of CREB5.
source: Together, we found TBX3 and NFIC were nuclear proteins associated with CREB5, FOXA1, and functionally impacted prostate cancer cell viability and ART resistance even absent of CREB5.
evidence: This is an inference based on RIME data, functional experiments, and genomic analysis.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC interacted specifically at FOXA1 motifs in cell lines.
source: In addition, they interacted specifically at FOXA1 motifs in cell lines, are amplified or overexpressed in prostate cancer patients, and their expression is associated with that of FOXA1 in mCRPC.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC are amplified or overexpressed in prostate cancer patients.
source: In addition, they interacted specifically at FOXA1 motifs in cell lines, are amplified or overexpressed in prostate cancer patients, and their expression is associated with that of FOXA1 in mCRPC.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of genomic and expression data from patient samples.

claim: The expression of TBX3 and NFIC is associated with that of FOXA1 in mCRPC.
source: In addition, they interacted specifically at FOXA1 motifs in cell lines, are amplified or overexpressed in prostate cancer patients, and their expression is associated with that of FOXA1 in mCRPC.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of expression data from mCRPC samples.

claim: The 335 proteins that bound both CREB5 and FOXA1 associated with AR, cell cycle, as well as Notch, Wnt, and SMAD/TGFβ pathways.
source: Based on the top 10 statistically significant signatures, we found that these 335 interactions associated with AR, cell cycle, as well as Notch, Wnt, and SMAD/TGFβ pathways (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: CREB5 overexpression was significantly associated with enrichment of signaling pathways EMT and β-catenin in the AR-positive LNCaP and LAPC4 cells, but not in the AR-negative cell lines PC3 and DU145.
source: We found that CREB5 overexpression was significantly associated with enrichment of signaling pathways EMT and β-catenin, the Wnt transcription effector in the AR-positive LNCaP and LAPC4 cells, but not in the AR-negative cell lines PC3 and DU145.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: In clinical mCRPC samples, CREB5 expression was correlated with the expression of EMT and β-catenin signaling programs.
source: In mCRPC, we found that CREB5 expression was correlated with the expression of similar signaling programs we found in vitro, including EMT (Alumkal et al., 2020; He et al., 2021) and β-catenin (Isaacsson Velho et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2015; Murillo-Garzón and Kypta, 2017; Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of RNA-seq data from mCRPC samples shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CREB5-associated nuclear protein interactions in cells and transcripts in mCRPC provide insights into the specific ART-resistant pathways that are activated by this transcription factor.
source: Together, the CREB5-associated nuclear protein interactions in cells and transcripts in mCRPC provide insights into the specific ART-resistant pathways that are activated by this transcription factor, showing the role CREB5 plays in regulating EMT and β-catenin signaling genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on RIME data, pathway enrichment analysis, and gene expression correlation analysis.

claim: CREB5 plays a role in regulating EMT and β-catenin signaling genes.
source: Together, the CREB5-associated nuclear protein interactions in cells and transcripts in mCRPC provide insights into the specific ART-resistant pathways that are activated by this transcription factor, showing the role CREB5 plays in regulating EMT and β-catenin signaling genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on pathway enrichment analysis and gene expression correlation analysis.

claim: FOXA1 promotes prostate cancer progression and resistance to ART and ADT.
source: We and others have demonstrated that transcription regulators, such as FOXA1, promote prostate cancer progression and resistance to ART and ADT.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and the authors' previous work.

claim: Overexpressed CREB5 exhibited shifts in binding at transcription regulatory elements as well as interaction with co-factors when cells were challenged with enzalutamide.
source: Our work identified other molecular events associated with transition towards resistance to second-generation ART and ADT. We did so by identifying reprogramming events associated with overexpressed CREB5, which exhibited shifts in binding at transcription regulatory elements as well as interaction with co-factors when cells were challenged with enzalutamide.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RIME data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In promoting proliferation in ART, CREB5 exhibited a strong degree of interaction with known AR transcription machinery, including FOXA1, HOXB13, and GRHL2, as well as novel prostate cancer regulators TBX3 and NFIC.
source: In promoting proliferation in ART, CREB5 exhibited a strong degree of interaction with known AR transcription machinery, including FOXA1, HOXB13, and GRHL2, as well as novel prostate cancer regulators TBX3 and NFIC.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The robust convergence of CREB5-FOXA1 function was observed through binding of transcription regulatory elements and interactions among nuclear proteins.
source: The robust convergence of CREB5-FOXA1 function was observed through binding of transcription regulatory elements and interactions among nuclear proteins.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RIME data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC interacted with CREB5 but required an intact B/L-Zip domain.
source: The factors TBX3 and NFIC interacted with CREB5 but required an intact B/L-Zip domain.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data comparing wild-type and mutant CREB5.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC, two nuclear factors that are amplified or overexpressed in mCRPC, were vulnerabilities in other prostate cancer models, including ones that were ART resistant.
source: TBX3 and NFIC, two nuclear factors that are amplified or overexpressed in mCRPC, were vulnerabilities in other prostate cancer models, including ones that were ART resistant, and bound to FOXA1 transcription regulatory elements.
evidence: This is supported by functional experiments and ChIP-seq data.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC bound to FOXA1 transcription regulatory elements.
source: TBX3 and NFIC, two nuclear factors that are amplified or overexpressed in mCRPC, were vulnerabilities in other prostate cancer models, including ones that were ART resistant, and bound to FOXA1 transcription regulatory elements.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Informatics modeling of the CREB5 activity through protein interactions and mCRPC transcription patterns indicated that CREB5 is associated with pathways found in patients resistant to enzalutamide.
source: Informatics modeling of the CREB5 activity through protein interactions and mCRPC transcription patterns indicated that CREB5 is associated with pathways found in patients resistant to enzalutamide (Alumkal et al., 2020; He et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis and gene expression correlation analysis, as well as cited studies.

claim: The dynamic binding properties of CREB5 mediate assembly of essential factors to AR and FOXA1 to promote resistant transcripts.
source: Altogether, our study indicates that the dynamic binding properties of CREB5 mediate assembly of essential factors to AR and FOXA1 to promote resistant transcripts (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq, RIME, and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: FOXA1 functions as an oncogenic pioneering and transcription factor in cancers, including prostate and breast.
source: FOXA1 functions as an oncogenic pioneering and transcription factor in cancers, including prostate and breast (Gerhardt et al., 2012; Nakshatri and Badve, 2009; Shah and Brown, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 is a critical dependency in prostate cancer cell line models.
source: FOXA1 is a critical dependency in prostate cancer cell line models (Pomerantz et al., 2015), including those that transdifferentiate into AR-agnostic, neuroendocrine-like features (Baca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: FOXA1 is a critical dependency in prostate cancer cell line models that transdifferentiate into AR-agnostic, neuroendocrine-like features.
source: FOXA1 is a critical dependency in prostate cancer cell line models (Pomerantz et al., 2015), including those that transdifferentiate into AR-agnostic, neuroendocrine-like features (Baca et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: EMT is associated with neuroendocrine prostate cancers.
source: Although EMT is associated with neuroendocrine prostate cancers (Beltran et al., 2016), AR-expressing mCRPCs that become enzalutamide resistance also show expression of EMT markers (Alumkal et al., 2020; He et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: AR-expressing mCRPCs that become enzalutamide resistant also show expression of EMT markers.
source: Although EMT is associated with neuroendocrine prostate cancers (Beltran et al., 2016), AR-expressing mCRPCs that become enzalutamide resistance also show expression of EMT markers (Alumkal et al., 2020; He et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The interactions of CREB5 and FOXA1 act as one mechanism that promotes EMT signaling in AR-positive-resistant cells.
source: Together, the work presented herein demonstrates that the interactions of CREB5 and FOXA1 act as one mechanism that promotes EMT signaling in AR-positive-resistant cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript showing CREB5-FOXA1 interactions and association with EMT pathways.

claim: TBX3 and NFIC interacted and correlated with FOXA1 in the setting of ART resistance based on RIME experiments and gene expression profile analyses of mCRPC samples.
source: We also found that TBX3 and NFIC interacted and correlated with FOXA1 in the setting of ART resistance based on RIME experiments and gene expression profile analyses of mCRPC samples.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data and gene expression correlation analysis.

claim: TBX3 expression has been shown to be required for viability of breast cancer cells.
source: Independent of CREB5 and FOXA1, TBX3 expression has been shown to be required for viability of breast cancer cells (Amir et al., 2016; Krstic et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: NFI factors, NFIA/B/C/X, have previously been shown to interact with FOXA1 to promote the transcription of AR target genes.
source: In addition, NFI factors, NFIA/B/C/X, have previously been shown to interact with FOXA1 to promote the transcription of AR target genes (Grabowska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Studies have identified increases in CREB5 as a marker for metastasis in ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancers.
source: Studies have identified increases in CREB5 as a marker for metastasis in ovarian, breast, and colorectal cancers (Bhardwaj et al., 2017; He et al., 2017; Molnár et al., 2018; Qi and Ding, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Bardwaj et al. have identified CREB5 transcripts as a repressed target of miRNA-29c, a tumor-suppressive miRNA lost in the triple-negative subtype of breast cancer.
source: Functionally, Bardwaj et al. have identified CREB5 transcripts as a repressed target of miRNA-29c, a tumor-suppressive miRNA lost in the triple-negative subtype of breast cancer (Bhardwaj et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Forced overexpression of CREB5 promoted cell cycle and colony formation in triple-negative breast cancer.
source: Forced overexpression of CREB5 promoted cell cycle and colony formation in this study.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study (Bhardwaj et al., 2017).

claim: Other CREB family members have been associated with therapy resistance in advanced prostate cancer.
source: While other CREB family members (Welti et al., 2021) have been associated with therapy resistance in advanced prostate cancer, the differential RIME interaction profiles displayed by these two family member proteins, CREB5 and CREB3, exhibited dichotomous behavior with respect to binding of nuclear proteins in cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The differential RIME interaction profiles displayed by CREB5 and CREB3 exhibited dichotomous behavior with respect to binding of nuclear proteins in cancer cells.
source: While other CREB family members (Welti et al., 2021) have been associated with therapy resistance in advanced prostate cancer, the differential RIME interaction profiles displayed by these two family member proteins, CREB5 and CREB3, exhibited dichotomous behavior with respect to binding of nuclear proteins in cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The oncogenic roles of CREB5 and other CREB family members may be distinct and mediated through their structurally different N-terminal domains.
source: This suggests that the oncogenic roles of CREB5 and other CREB family members may be distinct and mediated through their structurally different N-terminal domains.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in RIME profiles between CREB5 and CREB3.

claim: Experimental conditions, including cell culture and drug treatment, dramatically influenced CREB5 molecular interactions.
source: As another key observation, we also find that experimental conditions, including cell culture and drug treatment, dramatically influenced CREB5 molecular interactions.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RIME data showing changes in CREB5 binding and interactions under different conditions.

claim: TBX3 and NFCI have been previously detected in large-scale proteomic approaches that interrogated prostate cancer tissue.
source: As examples, TBX3 and NFCI have been previously detected in large-scale proteomic approaches that interrogated prostate cancer tissue (Sinha et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: TBX3 and NFCI have key regulatory roles in prostate cancer cell viability and ART resistance.
source: This study demonstrates that they have key regulatory roles in prostate cancer cell viability and ART resistance.
evidence: This is supported by functional experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibitors against EP300, an AR interacting protein, were efficacious in prostate cancer models.
source: Antagonizing nuclear or transcription factors has been efficacious in recent examples, as inhibitors against EP300, an AR interacting protein, were efficacious in prostate cancer models (Jin et al., 2017; Lasko et al., 2017; Welti et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: In regulating a pro-tumorigenic role in mCRPC, CREB5 requires additional factors including JUN/ATF and SWI/SNF complex.
source: In regulating a pro-tumorigenic role in mCRPC, CREB5 require additional factors (Supplementary file 1, Tables 2–4), including JUN/ATF and SWI/SNF complex.
evidence: This is supported by RIME data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SMARCB1 is a recurrent mutation in mCRPC.
source: Of bound SWI/SNF family members, we have previously discussed SMARCB1 as recurrent mutation in mCRPC (Armenia et al., 2018), and its loss as a biomarker in malignant pediatric tumors (Hong et al., 2019; Howard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Loss of SMARCB1 is a biomarker in malignant pediatric tumors.
source: Of bound SWI/SNF family members, we have previously discussed SMARCB1 as recurrent mutation in mCRPC (Armenia et al., 2018), and its loss as a biomarker in malignant pediatric tumors (Hong et al., 2019; Howard et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: CREB5 is a driver of mCRPC.
source: In summary, our observations implicate CREB5 as a driver of mCRPC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the manuscript showing CREB5's role in ART resistance and its interactions with key transcription factors.
